title: The root of all things
hook: the untaught make everything "mine", even nibbana; the monks were not pleased (MN 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Majjhima Nikaya, and your line, the middle length. Which title caught you, and did you read one thing all the way through? Day four hundred two.

Most of the discourses end the same way: the monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One's words. It's the canon's version of a standing ovation, again and again. The very first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends differently. The Buddha finishes speaking, and in the edition most translators follow, the text says plainly: the monks did not delight in what he said. First discourse. First page. Not pleased. Today: the root of all things.
screen: `MOST DISCOURSES END DELIGHTED.` → `THE FIRST ONE DOESN'T.` → `NOT PLEASED.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mulapariyaya, MN 1. The Buddha walks through everything a person could think of: earth, water, fire, air; beings and gods; the seen, the heard, the sensed, the known; unity and diversity; the all; and, last of all, nibbana. For each, he describes how an untaught person meets it. They perceive earth as earth. Then they conceive: they make earth into me, or put themselves in earth, or set themselves apart from earth; they think, earth is mine; and they delight in it. Why? Because, the Buddha says, they haven't fully understood it. The Pali verb is mannati: to conceive, to construe, to build a story with a self in it. And the startling part is the end of the list. Even nibbana, the end of grasping, can be made into a possession, conceived and delighted in. Then he describes someone in training, who knows earth directly as earth and is learning not to conceive. And the fully awakened, who don't conceive at all. Why weren't the monks pleased? The discourse doesn't say. A later commentary tells a story: these monks had been learned brahmins, proud of their scholarship, and the teaching was aimed at that pride. The Dhammapada makes a similar move in a single verse, in Max Müller's translation: “These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,” with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth? Not pleased is a fair place to start a book. Being bothered by a teaching sometimes means it found something.
screen: `EARTH, GODS, THE ALL, EVEN NIBBANA.` · `MANNATI — BUILDING A SELF-STORY.` · `KNOWING EARTH AS EARTH.` · `NOT PLEASED, ON PAGE ONE.` · then, large: `NOT PLEASED, YET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let things come: a sound, a feeling in the body, a thought. Watch for a small move that happens next: my knee, my plan, my noise, my problem. You don't have to stop it. Just notice the word mine arriving, a half second after the thing itself. Sound as sound. Then, mine. See if you can catch the gap between them. The bell holds the time.
Mannati, to conceive. How an untaught mind turns whatever it meets, even nibbana, into me and mine.
Your line: not pleased, yet. Today, when a teaching or an idea bothers you, don't throw it out; leave it on the table for a day. Day four hundred two.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics and scholars often study the Mulapariyaya Sutta as a famously difficult text; many teachers use it to point to the habit of making experience into 'me' and 'mine'.

fork.setup: the Buddha finishes the first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. how do the monks respond?
options: they delight in his words, as usual
they do not delight in his words
fork.reveal: they didn't delight. it's one of very few discourses that ends that way, and it sits on page one.

original.note: Pali maññati: to conceive, to construe; the verb MN 1 repeats for each thing the untaught make into 'me' and 'mine'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of philosophical categories.
what it means: how the mind turns whatever it meets into me and mine, even the highest goal.
what a scholar hears: the commentary says the listeners had been brahmins proud of their learning; its ending, 'the monks did not delight', is almost unique in the Pali discourses.
